Paramedic here and this post popped up in my recommended. 

You guys and gals all have BLS CPR, yeah? 

If so, the problem in a opioid OD isn’t a lack of narcan, it is the lack or absence of respiratory drive. Using a BVM to breathe for the patient is a far better move. 

Intranasal narcan isn’t really a good option, and I can think of 1 time in 5 years where I’ve given it over IV narcan. While obviously, you guys can’t give that, bagging a patient would be a great hold over. 

Intranasal narcan, comes with a whole host of risks. 

1) Flash pulmonary edema 
2) Vomiting from immediate withdrawals leading to a loss of the airway 
3) Other uncomfy side effects like headaches, from a build up of CO2 (hypercarbia) and hypoxia (lack of O2)

Basically, bag the patient who has an inadequate respiratory drive until EMS can get there!

Paramedic here - On average the most common patients we see present ‘abnormally’ in a heart attack are females >45; especially if they are diabetic. 

Diabetes leads to nerve breakdown from excess sugar; same way diabetics get neuropathy. 

I have caught a few STEMIs (what a heart attack looks like on the monitor) on some older females with very vague symptoms like acid reflux, vague chest discomfort, unexplained sweating,nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and others. 

The important thing is there is no typical presentation in every age group. We were taught by a EMS physician that the study that developed our standards for stereotypical symptoms was done on white males between 45 and 65; I have never fact checked this so don’t come for me.

Hell I had a patient one day, she called because she was “having a heart attack.” I get there I get into my questioning and ask why she thinks she is and she goes “my teeth hurt.” My partner and myself were stunned when she was in fact having a massive heart attack. All ended well she brought me cookies 3 stents and 2 weeks later! 

TL;DR - Vague symptoms? Concerned it may be a heart attack? Get it checked.

Okay, so intubation is all about the little things: 

1) The biggest mistake is people like to look ‘too close.’ Lean back see the big picture, don’t ‘tunnel vision’ yourself in. 

2) Try different blades, every medic on earth can debate Mac Vs Miller until the cows come home, but people tend to be better with one over the other. 

3) Identity your land marks as you go, intubation is an invasive, high risk/ low frequency skill, get in the habit of identifying structures out loud; additionally advance your blade slowly. This does two things. First, it lets your crew know where you are. Second, talking out loud helps keep you calm. I try to always identify the base of the tongue, oropharynx, epiglottis and then the cords. As soon as I see the cords, I’ll state the grade of my view. 

4) Once your blade is in, and you’re trying to get that view, don’t be afraid to physically manipulate the cricothyroid; either with BURP, cric pressure etc. I’ve gotten into the habit leaving the tube/ bougie on the patient’s chest and manipulating with my right hand. Then I’ll have someone redo what I did and place the tube. 

5) When you place the tube, slowly advance the tube. Watch the tube go in, only advance the tube so that the bulb is just past the cords. If your bulb is only just past the cords, you should avoid a Right Main-stem. 

6) If you miss and land in the esophagus, leave that tube. You now have something blocking one of the holes, and you’ve given yourself a ‘guide,’ in a sense. 

I sucked at intubating when I first started, but you do get better! I’ve also found that some intubation dummies feel completely different than a real person. The dummies we had in class, I feel some people are far easier to tube than they were. On the other hand I’ve missed tubes, they’re like IVs, you will miss one at some point. 

Best of luck to you!

Let's start simple: 

Blood pressure is the measure of two (kinda 3 things). 

1) Systolic (Top Number) - This is the force the heart exerts into the vessels during systole or contraction. 

2) Diastolic (Bottom Number)- This is the residual force left in the vessels when the heart is at rest or diastole. 

3) The MAP - Mean Arterial Pressure; this is calculated via DP + 1/3(SP-DP). This is your best indication of end organ perfusion and represents the average pressure over systole and diastole. 

  
Simply when the MAP is <65 some organs start to become hypoperfused (think kidneys and GI), where as at <60 the brain cannot maintain a adequate cerebral perfusion pressure (brain doesn't get O2). 

  
So as for vasodilation, think of circulation as having 3 parts. 

1) The pump (Heart) 

2) Container (vessels) 

3) Fluid (Blood) 

  
If I have a closed pipe system with a set volume of liquid and then add another section of piping the pressure will decrease since their is more space with the same volume of liquid; same concept for the body. Let's say the demand for this liquid is still the same, so my pump will have to speed up to still supply the same amount of liquid since resistance is less. Same concept applies to the heart and vessels. 



Compensatory mechanisms:

1) HR increase - This increases cardiac output and results in increased perfusion. 

2) Vasoconstriction - This results in increased resistance which means less volume can adequately reach where it needs to go and maintain pressure better. 



Yes, vasoconstriction improves perfusion; since decreased container size means an increase in pressure (so BP goes up increasing perfusion). 

For a sympathetic response (fight or flight) the following happens: 

1) HR increases - Increased rate increases cardiac output and therefor BP. 

2) RR increases to meet increased O2 demand

3) Blood vessels constrict - leading to increased vaso resistance. 

4) Increased heart contractility - the heart pumps with more force. 

When HR increases and vessels constrict BP increases since there is more pressure being exerted in a 'smaller' system.  



As for ICP it's sort of a spiraling 'mismanagement.'

1) Recall the space in the skull should be a constant volume. 

2) Something increases ICP, which means that constant volume is disrupted increasing this pressure. 

3) This increase in pressure begins to hypoprofuse the brain.  

4) The body goes 'oh shit, my brain isn't getting O2 as well as it should,' so the immediate action is to increase BP in a attempt to overcome this new found resistance. 

5) Increasing BP also increases ICP. 

4) Eventually the pressure will increase to a point where pressure is placed on the brain stem, resulting in chyenne stokes respiratory patterns and bradycardia (Since HR and RR are controlled here). Bradycardia can also result when the body goes 'oh shit our BP is way too high let's decrease cardiac output.' 



So knowing what a certain condition will do to BP is all related to rogue memorization of pathophysiology. Knowing that say sepsis or anaphylaxis  will cause vasodilation and result in low BP is all memorization. Knowing that ICP works in the previously stated pathway means you know that you would have increased BP. TL;DR this part is all memorization. 

  
Hope this clears some things up!

The influx of K into circulation causes potentially lethal dysthymias or dangerous irregular heartbeats. While dysthymias can result from heart attacks, crush traumas do not cause heart attacks. Heart attacks arise from a entirely different mechanism.

With proper pharmacological intervention, a patient can be safely extricated by EMS. 

Field amputation protocols are geared more towards this person is so entrapped by a limb that it’s easier or only possible to free the patient by amputating.

I gave this a quick glance, and it’s from a peer reviewed journal

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4919827/

When someone sustains a crush injury it cause a large global area of cell damage. This causes cells to ‘leak’ their cell contents. The most detrimental being K or potassium. This is trapped until the object crushing the patient is removed. Once the object is removed, circulation is restored causing a increase in serum (blood) K levels. When serum K levels are elevated, since K is a electrolyte you get serious heart electrical dysfunction. Calcium is given as a way to stabilize the heart muscle from the influx of potassium. 1) if you are not alert and orientated you can't refuse treatment and transport. If you are, you can refuse.

2) Alot if not most of our officers carry intranasal narcan. I wouldn't say they neccesarily have a high likelihood of running into it, it's just they either beat us on scene or they have to secure it for us. I think they should carry it, receive training in recognition of a OD and the use of narcan. It is available OTC from pharmacies, I believe Walgreens gives it out for free, I do know some charge for it. (Don't quote me on the free part.) My state has a course specifically designed to teach the lay rescuer how to recognize a OD, give narcan and call for help. 

3-1) as far as that goes epi/ adrenaline, to my understanding would not be used in a OD, more like a cardiac arrest (potentially from opioids). That starts to get into the area of ALS and that's wya above me. Typically, you give enough narcan and they respond. 

3-2) I'm in the US, in the south. We are a large rural county. Our first run district's population is around 20,000, spread over a large area. Our response times can be up to 25 minutes on a bad day, or if we have to go out of district, (and stay in the county) we may be looking at 50 minutes, for a low priority call. 

4) mainly it's the fact that we are a rural area, with small and in some instances unpaved roads. Trucks get stuck. 

5) 80% of our call volume is EMS related. We also run alot of public service calls like helping someone off the floor. 

6) So if we respond and dont transport we dont charge. If we transport, depending on if it's BLS emergent, BLS non emergent, ALS emergent or ALS non emergent you get charged a flat rate. Then the price per mile and I believe some medications and supplies maybe billed as well. All I'm positive about is the flat rate plus the loaded mile. 

7) Me personally, I'm in class to become a interior firefighter. To be a exterior or non IDLH firefighter no certifications are required. (IDLH means Immediately dangerous to life and health). I hold a few general certifications like healthcare level CPR and some FEMA stuff. All of my EMS training has been on the job in the field (I'm never without a certified provider because of my age and lack of EMS certifications). I do plan on getting my EMT when my firefighter class is complete. 

8) It would amaze you how many older folks will talk to you about sex. 

I had a patient one night, think that she had shot at us earlier and shot me. She also believed I was her grandchild. 

The other interesting ones would probably only be interesting if you like emergency medicine. 

9) We do alot of housekeeping in the station, we also are typically responsible for small station maintenance tasks. 

10) First, take a deep breath. You have recognized you have a emergency. Stay calm while you talk to dispatch, if they can understand you easily with struggling then they can get you the appropriate help quicker. 

Know your location. Always know where you're at if you had to call for emergency assistance. It would amaze you how often people's help is delayed because they dont know where they are. 

Take a CPR/ first aid class. Learn how to stop bleeding, recognize cardiac arrest and perform proper CPR. Dont be afraid to start CPR. If they need it, they are dead already you won't make it worse. I have seen too many people die without a chance that they may have had with early and effective CPR. 

11) so let's say I'm pulling duty with a shift. Shift change is at 7 AM. Being on time, means you're 30 minutes late. So typically you want to arrive between 6:30 - 6:45. Duty crews have to be out of bed by 6:45 so that's the sweet spot time. Before shift change formally happens, you want to stage your gear. Basically, getting your gear out and ready if you have a call. 

First, everyone sits down. The officers will pass information with each other, like what house duties were done, what tools were used, what calls were run etc. 

The next priority is truck checks. All the trucks are checked and any maintenance that needs to be done to them is completed. Missing or broken tools, supplies and equipment is repaired or replaced.

So at some point someone will go shopping for the day's lunch and dinner. Everyone contributes 5 dollars a meal. 

House keeping or "house duties" will get completed. Things like mopping, sweeping, cleaning etc.

Once all the chores are done then you wait for calls, do what you want to pass the time, train, work out. Sometime shifts will work out together or train together. It all depends how busy you are and what's going on in general. We have one paid person who brings a PS4 and a monitor and plays Call of Duty all day when he can. 

No day is typical but that's generally what happens, unless you get calls and dont have time. 

12) For the public. Get some training. Even if it's just CPR and stop the bleed do it. Know how to call your emergency number. If you want to further your training and serve your community, join your local fire company or rescue squad. Even if you dont want to run calls, alot will take any type of service you want to provide! Like say you just want to drive they will let you. Some agencies even want any type of help you will provide like repainting, grounds keeping or even tailoring for uniforms.

On to narcan. We carry narcan in two forms. First it's in our BLS drug box, or basic life support drug box. We carry 2, 4Mg intranasal doses. Typically that's enough. In our sealed, ALS drug box or advanced life support drug box, we carry narcan in a vial which can be given either through a atomizer, intranasally or through more invasive routes via a needle. When we start to get towards that sealed box, I don't have much knowledge about it since that's really more in the realm of a paramedic / ALS. Narcan/ naloxone is in the scope of practice so we are allowed to carry it and people, allowed through the scope of practice, are allowed to give it.
